$comment: Reviewed score of NIST PKITS: every accepted disagreement with the sentence that makes it acceptable, and the tests pinned on their PkiReasonCode rather than on the boolean. Expectations come from the file names, which is the only machine-readable statement of intent the archive carries — the PDF is transcribed, never parsed. Rescore with `npx tsx scripts/validate-certs.ts --update-baseline`, then WRITE the `why` of every new deviation by hand; the tool never fills one in, and an empty one fails the gate.

InvalidDNandRFC822nameConstraintsTest29.why:
RFC 5280 §7.1 says two distinguished names match when they compare equal after LDAP string preparation — case folded, whitespace collapsed, and across `PrintableString` and `UTF8String` alike. **pkinative compares encoded bytes**, everywhere and deliberately, and says so in every module that touches a name.

That is a conformance deviation and it is the one modern implementations share: Go's `crypto/x509` compares `RawIssuer` and `RawSubject` with `bytes.Equal`, and webpki does the same. The reason is that byte equality is the only comparison under which a cross-signed pair is decidable: two CAs that print the same name and encode it differently are two CAs, and a validator that merged them chooses a chain by accident. The direction of the miss is refusal — pkinative rejects a path a §7.1 validator accepts — which is why it costs availability rather than security, and why x509-limbo, written for the Web PKI, scores 99.44 % on the same code. Here the same rule reaches a name constraint rather than the chain: §7.1 preparation is what would make the constrained directoryName match the subject, and byte comparison does not. The direction is inverted for a constraint — a name that does not match is a name not excluded — so this one is an acceptance rather than a refusal, and it is the same missing comparison.

InvalidSeparateCertificateandCRLKeysTest.why: Who may **sign** a CRL, which is a different question from which certificates a list covers. The CA here issues a dedicated CRL-signing certificate and the list under test is signed by one of its other keys; the designation lives in the CRL's own `authorityKeyIdentifier`, and the certificate names no `cRLDistributionPoints` and no `cRLIssuer`, so nothing in the certificate points at a signer either. `verifyCertificateChain` accepts a signature from any certificate carrying the CA's encoded name and asserting `cRLSign` (RFC 5280 §4.2.1.3), which is exactly what makes a key rollover work and what, without matching the list's `authorityKeyIdentifier` against a candidate's key identifier, cannot tell a designated signer from an undesignated sibling. Matching it is a small and well-defined change — `computeKeyIdentifier` already exists — and it belongs to its own measurement rather than to the scoping work these tests were grouped under.

InvaliddeltaCRLTest4.why: RFC 5280 §5.2.4 **delta CRLs** are not applied. A delta lists what changed since a base list identified by its `BaseCRLNumber`, and it is only meaningful together with that base: read on its own it reports every certificate absent from it — which is nearly all of them — as unrevoked. So `crl-scope.ts` refuses to answer from a delta at all, which is the honest description of a feature that is not there rather than a reading anybody defends. Refusing errs in **both** directions, and PKITS has one test for each: a revocation recorded only on a delta is missed, and a revocation a delta lifted is still reported. Only applying the base and the delta together fixes either, and that is the next revocation piece. Here the certificate is revoked **on the delta only**, the base list is clean, and pkinative answers from the base — so it accepts a certificate PKITS says to refuse. This is the permissive direction of the gap and the reason the piece is scheduled rather than left: a CA that publishes revocations on deltas between base issuances has a window in which this library will not see them. It is recorded alone, and it is the one deviation in this baseline that accepts something a standards body says to reject.

ValidDSAParameterInheritanceTest5.why: DSA. Web Crypto implements no DSA at all, so `resolveAlgorithm` maps the signature to nothing and `verifyCertificateSignature` reports that the question could not be put — `PKI_REASON_SIGNATURE_NOT_CHECKED`, never `INVALID`. pkinative implements no signature algorithm of its own by construction (AGENTS.md: no secret-dependent cryptography in TypeScript, ever), so this is not a gap that closes; it closes only if a runtime grows DSA, which none is going to. NIST's suite predates that consensus. This one also needs parameter inheritance, where a certificate omits its DSA parameters and takes the issuer's — a shape that exists only for DSA.

ValidSelfIssuedinhibitAnyPolicyTest9.why: RFC 5280 §6.1.4 (h) exempts a **self-issued** certificate from spending the three policy counters, and §6.1.4 (j) decrements `inhibit_anyPolicy` for every certificate that is not self-issued. pkinative implements the exemption for the counters and still refuses this path with `PKI_REASON_NO_VALID_POLICY`, so one step of §6.1.5's wrap-up is reading the tree differently from NIST here. It is the only policy deviation of the 26, and the only one of them that is a suspected defect rather than a feature that is absent — which is why it is recorded alone rather than folded into a group.

ValiddeltaCRLTest5.why: RFC 5280 §5.2.4 **delta CRLs** are not applied. A delta lists what changed since a base list identified by its `BaseCRLNumber`, and it is only meaningful together with that base: read on its own it reports every certificate absent from it — which is nearly all of them — as unrevoked. So `crl-scope.ts` refuses to answer from a delta at all, which is the honest description of a feature that is not there rather than a reading anybody defends. Refusing errs in **both** directions, and PKITS has one test for each: a revocation recorded only on a delta is missed, and a revocation a delta lifted is still reported. Only applying the base and the delta together fixes either, and that is the next revocation piece. Here the deltas lift a certificate from `certificateHold` with the `removeFromCRL` reason that only a delta may carry, and pkinative answers from the base list alone — so it reports a revocation that was withdrawn. This is the same gap inverted: a certificate refused that PKITS says is good, which is the safe direction and still the wrong answer.
